title: Structs, embedding, tags, value vs reference semantics
summary: A struct is a value: assignment copies its fields, shallowly. Embedding promotes another type's fields and methods without inheritance or virtual dispatch, and tags attach metadata that encoding/json and database libraries read through reflection.

examples.title: Struct values, comparison, map keys, shallow copies

annotations.note: The zero value is a usable Point, with no constructor. Keyed literals keep compiling when fields are added; positional ones like Point{3, 4} are fine only for small, stable types, and vet flags them for struct types from other packages. q := p copies the struct, so q.X = 100 leaves p alone.
== compares field by field when every field is comparable, so a struct makes a natural composite map key, without the hashCode and equals pair Java needs.
The copy is shallow: r2 got its own Name but shares the Stops array with r1, so r1 sees {9 9}. Route has a slice field, which also makes r1 == r2 a compile error: slices are not comparable.
An anonymous struct type for a one-off shape, the standard layout of a table-driven test. %+v prints field names.
struct{} occupies no memory, so map[string]struct{} is the idiomatic set; the comma-ok read is the membership test.

examples.title: Embedding promotes fields and methods, without virtual dispatch

annotations.note: This is the difference from inheritance. Summary's receiver is the embedded Audit, which knows nothing about Order, so a.Label() calls Audit.Label even when reached through o: "audit v2", not "order 7". There is no template method by overriding; use an interface field or a function value.
An embedded field has a type and no name; its name is the type's name, so o.Audit is still reachable. Audit's fields and methods are promoted: o.By and o.Touch work as if Order declared them.
A method declared on Order hides the promoted one with the same name: the shallowest depth wins, for fields and methods alike.

New in Go 1.27: promoted fields can be keys in a composite literal. Before, you wrote Order{ID: 7, Audit: Audit{By: "ayşe", Version: 1}}; the compiler reports the version needed if the go line is older, and go fix's embedlit modernizer rewrites the old form once it isn't.
Touch has a pointer receiver. o is addressable, so o.Touch means (&o.Audit).Touch and changes o's embedded Audit in place.

examples.title: Struct tags drive encoding/json and database mapping

annotations.note: A tag is a raw string literal of key:"value" pairs; the compiler doesn't interpret it, and go vet's structtag check catches malformed ones. json renames fields; db is read by libraries such as pgx or sqlx.

omitempty drops false, 0, "", nil and empty collections, but never a struct, so the zero Joined time is still written. omitzero (Go 1.24) drops zero values and uses an IsZero method when the type has one, as time.Time does.
json:"-" keeps a field out of JSON entirely. That is the tool for exported fields; unexported ones are skipped anyway.

encoding/json falls back to a case-insensitive match, so "NAME" fills Name. encoding/json/v2 (Go 1.27) matches exactly unless you pass MatchCaseInsensitiveNames. If a client sends both "name" and "NAME", v1 keeps whichever comes last, without an error.
Tag.Lookup separates "absent" from "empty". This loop is, in miniature, how a row-to-struct mapper finds its column names.

use_cases: Domain records, request and response bodies, configuration: a struct per shape
Composite map keys: map[Point]int, map[struct{ user, day string }]int
Mixing in shared fields and helpers (timestamps, audit info, a sync.Mutex) by embedding
Mapping to JSON and database columns with tags instead of hand-written conversion code
strengths: Values by default: a copied struct can't be changed behind your back (except through its pointer, slice and map fields), unlike Java objects, which are always references
Comparable structs work with == and as map keys with no equals/hashCode to write or get wrong
Embedding reuses fields and methods without a class hierarchy; there is no fragile base class, because the embedded type never calls back into the outer one
Tags keep wire names and column names next to the field they describe, like Java annotations but read only at runtime through reflect
weaknesses: Copies are shallow and silent: a struct with a slice or map field shares that data with every copy
Tags are unchecked strings: a typo like json:"naem" or a missing colon compiles; go vet catches syntax, not misspelled names
Embedding exposes the embedded type's whole method set, so embedding *sync.Mutex or a big type widens your API by accident
Large structs passed by value cost a copy on every call; pass pointers when they are big or must be mutated

pitfalls.title: Expecting virtual dispatch through embedding
pitfalls.detail: A method of the embedded type always calls the embedded type's methods. If behavior must vary, put an interface or a func field in the struct.

pitfalls.title: Modifying a copy in a range loop
pitfalls.detail: for _, o := range orders { o.Total = 0 } changes copies. Index instead, or store pointers.

pitfalls.title: omitempty on a struct or time.Time field
pitfalls.detail: It never omits structs, so a zero time is encoded as 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z. Use omitzero (Go 1.24) or a pointer field.

pitfalls.title: Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex
pitfalls.detail: The copy gets its own, possibly locked, mutex and protects nothing. go vet's copylocks check reports it; pass such structs by pointer.

quiz.q: type Base struct{}; func (Base) Name() string { return "base" }; func (b Base) Hello() string { return b.Name() }. type D struct{ Base } with its own Name returning "d". What does D{}.Hello() return?
quiz.why: Hello's receiver is the embedded Base, so it calls Base.Name. Embedding promotes methods; it doesn't make them virtual.

quiz.q: r2 := r1 where Route has Name string and Stops []Point. After r2.Stops[0] = p, what does r1.Stops[0] hold?
quiz.why: Assignment copies the slice header, not the array; both Routes share Stops.

quiz.q: Which struct can be used as a map key?
quiz.why: Map keys must be comparable; slices and maps aren't, and neither is a struct containing them.

quiz.q: A time.Time field tagged json:"at,omitempty" holds the zero time. What does json.Marshal do?
quiz.why: omitempty doesn't apply to structs. omitzero does, using time.Time's IsZero method.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Struct types
The Go Programming Language Specification: Composite literals

body:
## Concept

A struct is a sequence of named fields, and a struct value *is* its fields: no header,
no hidden pointer, no identity. Assigning, passing or returning a struct copies every
field. That copy is shallow: pointer, slice and map fields are copied as references,
so the copy shares what they point to. A struct is comparable with `==`, and usable as
a map key, when all its fields are.

**Embedding** a type (a field with a type but no name) promotes its fields and methods
to the outer struct, so `o.By` means `o.Audit.By` and `o.Touch()` means
`o.Audit.Touch()`. It is composition with shorter syntax: the embedded value never
learns about the struct around it, so there is no overriding and no virtual dispatch.
Polymorphism comes from interfaces instead.

**Tags** are string literals after a field's type. The compiler ignores them;
packages such as `encoding/json` read them through `reflect` to choose names and
options.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Java**: there are no classes, only structs with methods. Values instead of
  references by default, `==` instead of `equals`/`hashCode`, embedding instead of
  `extends` (without `super` and without overriding), tags instead of annotations.
- **C**: a struct is laid out like a C struct and copied by value, as in C. Embedding
  is the "first member is the base struct" trick, made official and given promoted
  names.
- **C++**: closest to a struct with public members. Embedding resembles inheritance
  in which no method is `virtual`, minus the implicit upcast: an `Order` is not an
  `Audit`, you pass `o.Audit` explicitly.
- **Python/JS**: no dynamic attributes; the field set is fixed at compile time. A JS
  object spread `{...a}` is shallow in the same way a Go struct copy is.

## Design notes

Make the zero value useful (`var buf bytes.Buffer` works, so should your types), and
prefer keyed literals so adding a field never breaks callers. Embed to reuse
behavior you would otherwise forward method by method, but only when the embedded
type's whole method set belongs in your API; otherwise use a named field. When a
struct holds a mutex, slices that must not be shared, or is large, give it pointer
methods and pass `*T`. Tags are a contract with another system (an API, a table):
keep them stable, test them with a round trip, and remember that `encoding/json`
matches names loosely while `encoding/json/v2` is strict.
